22. Define leukoplakia. What are the clinical types of leukoplakia?
Leukoplakia is defined as a white patch or plaque that cannot be characterized clinically or histologically as any other lesion.
Types of leukoplakia
• Homogeneous: Uniformly white patch with slightly raised mucosa (cracked mud appearance) • Proliferative verrucous leukoplakia (PVL) is an aggressive form of oral leukoplakia that is persistant and refractory to treatment with a high-risk of malignant transforma- tion, begins as benign hyperkeratotic lesion and often becomes multifocal.
• Nodular lesion: White lesion with granular surface associated with candida infections. • Speckled leukoplakia: Combined red and white lesions with irregular surface.

nodes.title: 78. What are typical and atypical target lesions?
nodes.summary: The text describes typical and atypical target lesions in erythema multiforme and related conditions, and defines centripetal versus centrifugal spread with examples. Typical target lesions are acral, bullseye-like lesions pathognomonic for erythema multiforme, with concentric zones and central epidermal damage. Atypical target lesions are more common in SJS/TEN, usually truncal, and have central blisters and poorly defined borders. Centripetal spread is toward the center/axis, while centrifugal spread is away from it. Examples include centripetal spread in erythema multiforme, Rocky Mountain spotted fever, staphylococcal TSS, varicella/chickenpox, ACLE, and rare trigeminal spread of squamous cell carcinoma; centrifugal spread occurs in variola and rabies virus, and varicella reactivation causing shingles.

nodes.title: Systemic Corticosteroid Regimens for Oral Lesions
nodes.summary: The page describes systemic corticosteroid therapy for autoimmune and immune-based inflammatory diseases, especially oral lesions. It opens by noting that these diseases are generally incurable and treatment aims for prolonged remission. Three systemic corticosteroid regimens are covered. Regimen I, the preferred regimen, is indicated for pemphigus vulgaris, erosive lichen planus, and severe non-ocular pemphigoid, with a detailed prednisone schedule: a 100–120 mg/day loading dose for 2 weeks, gradual tapering to 20 mg/day, then 10 mg/day, then every-other-day dosing, and eventual discontinuation. Its rationale includes rapid suppression, reduced side effects at lower doses, prevention of exacerbations, and recovery of the adrenal axis. Regimen II is used for resistant pemphigus, selected lupus or sarcoidosis, and is preferred for Stevens-Johnson erythema multiforme; it uses the same initial high dose but stops abruptly after 2 weeks, offering simpler management but with more frequent exacerbations and less disease control. Regimen IIIA is for severe cases not controlled by lower doses, using high-dose prednisone followed by tapering to the lowest effective dose; many patients need long-term high doses, lifelong follow-up, and may experience late complications of ongoing corticosteroid therapy.

nodes.title: 63. What are the disadvantages of paralleling angle technique?

For studying of mandibular third molar impaction this technique is used. This

technique is developed in 1952. The steps are as follows: 1. The film is places as far back as possible and the patient is asked to bite gently. 2. To make angle prominent the head is tilted downwards and forwards. 3. The central ray is perpendicular to film. Impacted third molars are visualized in buccal and lingual plane. 71. What is umbra and penumbra?
The word penumbra is derived from two Latin words pene means almost and umbra means shadow. The region of complete image is called umbra. Penumbra is the region of partial illumination that surrounds the umbra or complete shadow. It is also called geometric unsharpness or edge gradient.

nodes.title: 71. What is umbra and penumbra?

nodes.title: 72. What is latent image?
nodes.summary: The text explains the formation of the latent image in radiographic film through the Gurney-Mott hypothesis: X-ray photons interact with bromide ions, freeing electrons that are trapped at sensitivity sites and attract interstitial silver ions to form neutral silver atoms, creating latent image sites; development and fixation convert these into a visible radiograph with radiopaque and radiolucent areas. It also describes parallax as image unsharpness caused by viewing from different perspectives, double-emulsion image variation from the divergent X-ray beam, and distortion due to intensifying screen light crossing the film base.

nodes.title: Dental Radiography Darkroom and Safe Light Requirements
nodes.summary: The page covers dental X-ray darkroom requirements and safe light principles. It begins by mentioning that light-absorbing dyes can help and that parallax is more pronounced in wet films. The darkroom should be near the operatory, at least 4 × 5 feet, lightproof, locked, well-ventilated, and temperature-controlled to prevent film fogging. A safe light is a filtered darkroom lamp that permits limited handling of films because X-ray films are sensitive mainly to UV, blue, and green wavelengths. Safe light filters must match the film, be unscratched, use correct bulb wattage, be placed at least 4 feet away, and minimize exposure of pre-exposed films. The coin or penny test checks safe light fogging.

nodes.title: 2. Inferior alveolar canal
Classification
key_items: Benign Periosteal Reaction; Aggressive Periosteal Reaction
nodes.summary: The text describes periosteal reactions, including their occurrence, causes, classification, and specific patterns. It explains that periosteal reactions appear earlier and more aggressively in children, are rare in jaws, and occur after periosteal stripping. They are most common in osteomyelitis then malignant conditions, and absent intra-articularly. Reactions are classified as benign or aggressive: benign reactions are associated with slow chronic irritation and appear thick and wavy, while aggressive reactions result from rapid processes and appear lamellated, amorphous, or sunburst-like. Although no reaction is unique, uninterrupted lamellar reaction indicates a benign slow-growing process, while onion skin pattern indicates a more aggressive process with intermittent bone formation.

It also lists patterns associated with osteomyelitis, sarcomas, and odontogenic myxoma, and CT-based classification of adjacent cortical destruction. nodes.title: Teeth Conditions
nodes.summary: The text discusses radiographic sclerosis patterns and how tooth displacement/impaction and root resorption help in diagnosis. Benign tumors/cysts tend to show condensed sclerotic margins, whereas reactive lesions show diffuse sclerosis, with examples including cementomas, odontogenic myxoma, and myeloma. It also explains that lesions around unerupted tooth crowns are usually odontogenic; displaced unerupted teeth suggest specific benign or aggressive lesions, while nondisplaced impacted teeth indicate less aggressive processes such as odontoma. Root resorption patterns are also diagnostic: one or several root apices suggest benign aggressive disease, knife-edge resorption occurs in ameloblastoma, multiple root planes resorption in central giant cell granuloma, and spiking resorption suggests malignancy.
